question: Your rover holds two laser scans of the L-shaped room. Why can ICP not know the right point pairs in advance?
options: The dots have no labels, so it guesses nearest pairs
The scanner returns too few dots to form any pairs at all
Pairs are only defined once the robot has stopped moving
explanation: With no labels, nearest neighbour is the only available guess.

question: Your rover's ICP pairs dots and then runs an SVD step. What does the SVD step solve?
options: Which old dot is nearest to each new dot
The noise level of each laser beam over time
The best turn and shift for fixed pairs
explanation: Kabsch gives the optimal rigid fit for given correspondences.

question: Your rover's ICP fits a turn and a shift. Why force the last singular direction by the sign of a determinant?
options: To speed up the SVD by skipping a step
To average out the noise in the pairs
To rule out a mirrored fit of the points
explanation: An orthogonal fit may be a reflection, which is not a robot motion.

question: You start your rover's ICP 100 degrees away from the right answer in the L-shaped room. What is likely?
options: A crash from a singular matrix in the SVD
A local minimum with a large final error
explanation: Nearest points are wrong partners, so the fit locks in a wrong pose.

question: Your rover scans only one straight wall. Why does ICP fail?
options: The wall has too few points to give a mean
Every shift along the wall fits equally well
Real walls bend, so a rigid fit cannot match
explanation: The fit has no information about the slide along the wall.

question: You want your rover's ICP to succeed from farther away. What is the best way to widen its success range?
options: Start the fit from the wheel odometry guess
Add many more iterations from the same start
Use far fewer points so pairing gets easier
explanation: A close start keeps nearest points as true partners.
